items.lbText:
Gap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppers

High street brands that boomed in the noughties before the squeeze of both sustainably minded consumers and the rise of ultra-cheap online labels are staging a comeback.

This time, rather than focusing solely on trend-led affordable designs, the names familiar to any shopper are courting luxury fashion, A-list collaborations and enhanced services in an attempt to engage consumers.

Think Gap’s new collection with Victoria Beckham. Or Marks & Spencer showcasing a covetable catwalk collection at London fashion week with celebrities including Joan Collins and assorted gen Z Gallaghers in attendance, then making it available to buy immediately, with half of the pieces under £50. Topshop relaunched last year and now has concessions in 30 John Lewis stores, as well as the luxury retailer Liberty.

Lisa Illis, the head of design at M&S, describes their recent catwalk show as “making the buzz of London fashion week accessible to everyone”. She says “more fashion-informed seasonal collections” have seen the number of under-35s shopping at the retailer increase 16% year on year.

The Hollywood stylist Law Roach , whose clients include Zendaya, has been appointed stylist-in-residence at Asos, where his influence will be felt not just in advertising campaigns, but also through his suggestions on different items from across the site to wear together.

“In research, we found that 68% of consumers say what they need to know is how to wear something,” says Vanessa Spence, Asos’s executive vice-president of brand.

The online retailer has added AI stylists, virtual try-on tools and a Buy the Look option, which allows consumers to buy an outfit in one go, a feature that Spence says is very popular. “We’re helping customers find pieces that they want to wear. Then they can get more from every purchase and extend the life of their product.”

Ella Baynes, insight manager at retail consultants Savvy Marketing, says the shift shows brands are adapting to the more sophisticated ways consumers are approaching fashion, particularly online. “Instead of competing directly, [these retailers] are borrowing some of luxury fashion’s cultural cues,” she says. “You’re meeting both that shopper aspiration, but also the shopper reality [with the price].”

Asos’s extensive adaptive collection for disabled customers also shows this broader way of thinking. The company worked with disabled consultancy Tilting the Lens on the range. “There is an ability to develop, even for yourself, a capsule collection,” says founder and disability advocate Sinéad Burke, who has achondroplasia, the most common form of restricted growth. “It’s not just one suit, it’s not just one skirt, you can customise the pieces. You can wear the magnetic waistcoat with the pants. We hope what we’re giving people is greater choice.”

Crucially, these items are affordable – nothing is more than £65 – which is particularly important for disabled people, 46% of whom are not in work in the UK. “Whenever we’re looking at shopper attitude, cost is absolutely king,” confirms Baynes.

For Asos in particular, which registered a sharp decline in sales post-Covid and new competition from ultra-cheap brands like Shein, an overhaul was needed. Sales were down 12% last August . A cost-cutting drive, including charging for returns, helped the site turn a corner, and they announced a 50% growth of profits this March, although the impact of a cyber-attack at the beginning of October is yet to become clear.

Andrea Cheong, fashion commentator and author of Why Don’t I Have Anything to Wear?, regularly posts Instagram videos reviewing different items from affordable brands, in order to assess how well made they are. She has noticed that brands are not signposting their environmental credentials as much as they once did – due to a combination of criticism from campaigners, cost and the rise of conservatism. “It wasn’t something that was very lucrative once the economy was in decline, and then bring politics into it, that has a huge impact,” she says.

At M&S, which first launched its eco-commitments in 2007, value and sustainability are not competing priorities. “By designing pieces with longevity in mind, from everyday wardrobe staples to more fashion-led seasonal collections, we’re helping customers build wardrobes they’ll wear and love for longer,” says Illis.

But regardless of making more enduring styles, retailers are always up against changeable consumer behaviour – and damning statistics like the estimate that a garment is on average worn seven times before it is thrown away .

Even if brands are borrowing from the luxury playbook, the reality may not always match up, argues Cheong. “However much they try to elevate what it is, it is not the same [fabric] that they use at, for example, Dior.” The use of human-made fibres in ranges like the M&S catwalk collection and Asos Adaptive is just one example of the difference between high fashion and high street.

Cheong says a lot of gen Z and millennial customers are also shopping secondhand, with resale app Vinted now the third biggest retailer in the UK . “I would say 70% or 80% of my audience are 25 to 35 and they are really jaded. They are a lot more savvy than brands seem to think.”

Sustainability aside, perhaps this new shift shows that brands are realising consumers are more cynical now – and that they need to do more to reach their radar.

items.lbText:
We need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaply

J ohn Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget . The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say.

Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so.

Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now.

Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out.

More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential. Countries that once had a more communitarian approach, such as France and Germany, with a highly regulated mix of social, private rented and home ownership, have succumbed to building wealth through property.

It doesn’t seem to matter that Japan was ruined in the 1990s by a vicious property price crash. And China is still suffering domestically after Beijing allowed a property Ponzi scheme to develop that enriched the already super-wealthy and left tens of millions of middle-income earners in negative equity.

Nowhere is the situation worse than in the UK, where property prices have cooled somewhat, but remain at levels that deny younger generations the chance to find a home at a reasonable price and some financial security.

UK property has also become the method by which Gen Xers pay for social care for their parents and release housing deposits for their offspring. Then there is the debilitating leasehold /freehold split that is both a source of angry disputes and stymies investment in solar panels and insulation (who should pay?).

The lack of regulation and ill-thought-out subsidies affecting new private housing means developers are incentivised to enter an arm-twisting contest with local authorities. Without robust planning guidelines, developers champion building on flood plains or erecting tower blocks that are later dubbed ovens for their lack of ventilation in hot summers.

And all the while the tax system is working to make the situation worse.

The Oxford academic John Muellbauer has spent almost 40 years researching the UK’s housing system. He calls it “one of the most dysfunctional in the world”.

In an academic article published in September by the British Academy, he says: “Many of the UK’s current economic and social problems, including its housing affordability crisis, can be traced to decades of land and housing policy failures. The role of land markets is strongly dependent on institutions, including land use regulation, financial regulation and property taxation.”

The Treasury and Angela Rayner’s Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have considered proposals from Muellbauer and others that remodel council tax, turning it into a fairer annual levy on households and using the reform to abolish stamp duty on transactions, which has calcified the housing market.

Rachel Reeves’s mansion tax is a good start . It is only a start though, because the former chancellor was persuaded to keep the council tax banding system when she should have applied a percentage to the 150,000-odd homes valued above £2m that will be captured by the new policy.

There was the potential for a database of homes valued above £2m to be the beginning of a revaluation process, carrying on until all homes were logged. With a percentage tax of, say, 0.5%, applied to all homes, a £150,000 property would pay an annual tax rate of £750 while a £3m home would pay £15,000.

Of course, the real problem is not the £3m homeowner for whom policymakers will have little sympathy – it’s the professionals occupying £1.5m homes in London, the south-east and affluent suburbs around other big cities, who will see council tax rates more than double to £7,500.

The professional classes will be the worst affected in the short term. Yet there will only be progress when this powerful lobby group of owner-occupiers – working and retired – are prepared to accept the trade-off with stamp duty, which would disappear for those who sell.

There are plenty of people in government who understand the need to resolve housing market issues in a more fundamental fashion. The Treasury minister Torsten Bell is one. His book, Great Britain?: How We Get Our Future Back, talks about “our housing omnishambles”.

However, they have had little influence on policy in this area so far. In his first budget Healey revamped a much-discredited help-to-buy scheme for new-build homes, which will only boost prices and line the pockets of developers. He also gave some more money towards council housebuilding, slapped an extra tax on landlords (that will probably push up rents) and promised to tackle homelessness.

Healey and Andy Burnham put all their revolutionary zeal into a long, and possibly tortuous, process of devolution from London to the regions to kickstart growth.

However, it is tax incentives that are causing the problems, not whether policy decisions are made locally or centrally. Bad policy decisions can be made locally just as much as centrally. What makes the difference is a permanently reformed tax landscape that discourages treating housing as a store of wealth, allows people to move home cheaply – especially older homeowners who want to downsize – and supports the building of more truly affordable homes to buy and rent.

items.lbText:
Environmental Defense Fund analysis shows administration handed out $950m and Clean Air Act exemptions

It’s a good time to be a coal plant in the US. The Trump administration has given support to almost half of the nation’s coal plants, helping them to continue operating despite economic and regulatory headwinds, according to a new analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund.

The analysis, which looked at the 184 operating coal plants that are connected to the grid, found that 90 received support from the Trump administration through “cash handouts, free passes to pollute, and requirements to stay online past their retirement dates”.

The administration provided $950m in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and handed Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants, according to the EDF analysis.

“It’s extending the life of these coal plants,” said Surbhi Sarang, director and senior attorney at the Environmental Defense Fund. “The administration has leveraged a multitude of tools to prop up coal plants, and ultimately all of that is harming Americans even more by increasing electricity costs, by increasing pollution – it’s like Americans are getting hit twice.”

In 2015, the EPA’s Mercury and Air Toxics Standards first took effect, driving down dangerous pollution from power plants by more than 90%. In 2024, the EPA updated the standards to further reduce harmful pollution from coal-fired power plants. In the early days of the second Trump term, companies were invited to email the administration to request an exemption from the 2024 standards. According to emails obtained by the EDF through Freedom of Information Act requests, companies expressed concern that the standards would cost them too much money.

The Colstrip plant in Montana has operated for more than 40 years, affecting nearby communities like the Northern Cheyenne reservation by releasing toxic chemicals like mercury, arsenic, lead and nickel. “That’s one of the dirtiest coal plants that’s still operating in the nation,” Sarang said.

In 2024, the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for coal-fired power plants was strengthened in several ways. For example, the standard for fine particulate matter, or fPM, reduced allowable emissions of nickel, arsenic, lead and other toxic metals from coal plants by two-thirds. According to the EDF, NorthWestern Energy and Talen Energy, which own and operate the Colstrip plant, requested an exemption from the fPM requirement.

Brian Bird, president and CEO of NorthWestern, wrote an email to the Department of Energy in March 2025 asking for a 15-minute chat about the standards with administrator Lee Zeldin. In the email , obtained by EDF, he argued that it would cost $500m to comply with the new rule: “It is ludicrous that our customers would have to cover the costs of a $500m investment for such a slight improvement to particulate matter capture,” he wrote.

The Trump administration gave NorthWestern an exemption from complying with the 2024 updated standards, which the administration went on to repeal in February.

Sarang said the Colstrip plant had not installed modern pollution controls that could reduce emissions. If it had been required to comply with the 2024 updated standards, it would have had to upgrade its equipment, she said: “It would have had pretty significant impacts on air pollution.”

NorthWestern, which became Colstrip’s majority owner earlier this year, describes the coal plant as a “dependable bridge to a cleaner energy future” that supplies reliable energy “until viable, equivalent, carbon-free energy resources are commercially available”.

Asked to comment on EDF’s report, NorthWestern said its technology at the Colstrip plant is “state of the art” for removing sulphur dioxide, and is 99.6% efficient in removing filterable particulate emissions. The company said if the updated 2024 federal standards had taken effect, it would have required it to become 99.8% efficient by 2028, costing hundreds of millions of dollars. The company said its mercury emission control at the Colstrip plant meets current state and federal requirements.

Another coal plant that received a pass from the Trump administration is the WA parish coal plant outside of Houston, Texas. Community members living nearby have called for it to be shut down due to its planet-heating CO2 emissions and what they say are ‘hazardous’ levels of particulate matter.

The plant’s owner, NRG, asked the Department of Energy for an exemption for all of its coal-fired facilities including the WA parish plant, arguing that its facilities wouldn’t be able to comply with the new standards and would need to “derate in order to comply”, taking megawatts off the grid in “critical areas”, according to an email obtained by EDF. NRG wrote that complying with the regulations “with razor thin margins” would risk the affordability and reliability of the grid.

A 2018 Rice University study found that the plant is responsible for as many as 177 premature deaths each year from PM 2.5, which are particles small enough to enter the bloodstream through the lungs, causing increased rates of respiratory diseases, heart attacks and strokes. “Our research has shown that WA parish is the deadliest power plant in Texas,” explained Rice professor Daniel Cohan.

NRG did not respond to a request to comment.

Cohan said plants across the country were supposed to meet the 2024 updated standards. “Trump is letting them off the hook from the more stringent version of the standard,” he said.

“It lets them stay open longer,” Cohan explained. “Many coal plants in this country are barely on the edge of breaking even, and so any regulations that force them to spend more money to clean up their pollution is likely to cause some of them to choose to retire and be replaced by cheaper and cleaner sources.”…

items.lbText:
Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress

Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.

Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies .

Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transform humanity’s relationship with nature . Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets. The UK is set to meet just three of the 23.

After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade.

During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement.

“A lot of what’s going on out here at the Cop is just a bunch of baloney and beautiful speeches and BS,” he told AFP earlier this week. “We cannot have – we cannot expect – a consensus between every nation on Earth on every topic. That’s ridiculous. Cops have been designed to fail, and they are not disappointing.”

He also argued that the UN should host a single environmental Cop each year to tackle the climate, biodiversity, plastics and other issues in one go.

“This just makes my blood boil, because while we fiddle, Rome burns,” he said.

The negotiations in the Armenian capital have seen Argentina, Saudi Arabia and Russia water down language on environmental ambition in the final agreement, while wealthier governments were divided on who would contribute more financial resources.

European nations would like to see additions to the list of donor states, as China and several of the Gulf states are still classified as developing countries in the UN process despite decades of rapid economic development. The final agreement in Yerevan left this issue open.

Key decisions on a fund to mobilise resources from firms that make money from digital forms of biodiversity, such as pharmaceutical companies, were postponed to the next summit in Ecuador in two years’ time. It had been hoped that the fund would generate £1bn a year for nature conservation, with a significant share going to Indigenous communities, but it has so far raised just over $10,000.

The calls for changes to the biodiversity Cop process echo an intervention by leading policy experts during climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024 who said the summit was “no longer fit for purpose” and needed to shift to focus on implementation.

Ruth Davis, the UK’s nature envoy, said she recognised that the meetings could be “extremely frustratiing”, but a huge amount of implementation was happening around the world.

“We’ve got to make the system actually deliver outcomes for people, otherwise they’ll lose confidence in it,” she said. “In the end, this is a process that is owned by governments who are parties to it. But I know we are going to find friends and allies in making the process work for the citizens of countries for whom this is really important, not least because they are the ones facing the impacts.”

Efforts to reform the UN’s sprawling environmental agenda are already under way. Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, said that the current systems were driving change, but they were moving too slowly.

“Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen. “We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands.

“Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that.”

items.lbText:
London Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay open

Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works.

Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well as Birmingham New Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period.

Passengers travelling between London , north-east England and Scotland will have to negotiate the part closure of the east coast mainline on Christmas Eve. Direct trains from the capital to parts of Essex and Norfolk will also be cut for much of the festive period.

Network Rail said most routes would still stay open and that the Christmas period, when train services generally stop for 25 and 26 December, remained the best time to conduct essential works.

Engineers hope to use the quieter festive days to carry out about £152m of works to improve reliability and capacity.

The biggest engineering work is expected on the lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough. Most Great Western services to Wales and the west of England will start and finish at Reading, with some services diverting around Oxford to London Euston, from 27 December until 4 January.

The work also means Elizabeth line services west of Paddington and Heathrow Express services will not resume after Christmas until 31 January.

Birmingham’s main station, New Street, will be closed from the start of Christmas Eve until 29 December to replace overhead power supplies. No trains will stop or pass through, with rail replacement buses serving the city centre.

Passengers using east coast mainline services run by LNER and other operators may wish to avoid travel on Christmas Eve. Work at Doncaster means trains between London, north-east England and Scotland will be partly replaced by rail replacement buses from Newark to York, adding two hours to journeys.

The Great Eastern mainline out of London Liverpool Street will be closed for 10 days from Christmas Day for track replacement in east London, meaning no Greater Anglia or Elizabeth line rains will run through the area, with no direct trains from Norwich to London.

TransPennine services between Leeds and Manchester will be slowed for six weeks from Christmas Day with the closure of Huddersfield station.

Network Rail’s group director, system operator, Anit Chandarana, said: “Christmas is a time when many people want to be with family and friends, and most of the railway will be open to help them get there. We have worked with train operators to keep services running wherever we can on the busiest travel days and to provide alternative journey options where work affects the usual route.

“We are sorry that some passengers will face disruption. The days between Christmas and new year are by far the quietest of the year and give us the best opportunity to complete major projects such as the power supply upgrades at Birmingham and Paddington. Our teams will do everything they can to keep people moving, and we urge passengers to check their journeys before setting off.”

items.lbText:
Even modest overpayments can save you a fortune. We look at the best ways to pay off your biggest debt early

W hen Adrian Massey was made redundant from his job as a food developer in 2010, the bill that worried him the most was the mortgage. Just over a decade later he and his wife, Tulay, had cleared their debt early, saving themselves £30,000 and freeing up some money to start their own business.

The couple had bought their six-bedroom home in Banbury, Oxfordshire, for £280,000 two years before he lost his job.

With an interest rate on their mortgage of 6.1%, the couple’s monthly payment was about £1,400. “It felt like a burden; a chain around my neck,” says Adrian, 50. “I started thinking about the best way to pay it down.

“It dawned on me what could happen if you overpay even a relatively modest amount. You can really start to make a difference.”

When he started his next job he set up a standing order to overpay the mortgage. “We looked at our current income and outgoings, and then, based on our spare cash, we decided how much did we want to put into clearing the mortgage without overstretching ourselves,” he says.

They decided they could afford £500 a month. After that, any pay rises they received were funnelled into the mortgage, and the couple would sometimes add a lump sum of up to £2,000 from savings.

When their five-year, fixed rate deal ended in 2013, they remortgaged to a rate of 2.5%, choosing a tracker deal that had no limits on overpayments.

The extra they paid each month started to make an even bigger difference. By 2021, Adrian and Tulay were mortgage-free – seven years ahead of schedule.

“I know that, purely from a financial point of view, there are advantages to investing more in the stock market because of the returns you get, but the freedom was more important to me,” he says. “It has meant I have been able to invest in myself and the life I want to lead, rather than being shackled to this payment.”

The money that used to go into repayments has been used to set up a business, ATM Food Innovations, and Adrian has also upped his pension contributions.

“Making the final payment felt really good; it’s a real sense of relief and liberation,” he says. “You know that whatever happens, no one can take your house away.”

With interest rates rising, it is no wonder that achieving mortgage-free status is a goal for so many.

Andrew Hagger, finance expert at Moneycomms, says: “For most people, repaying the mortgage means getting rid of the biggest financial commitment hanging around your neck.

“They dream of what they could do with all the extra disposable income: holidays, update the car, home improvements, or retire early. The list is endless.”

Clearing your mortgage not only means removing what is likely to be your largest monthly expense, it can also save you thousands of pounds in interest that would have been paid over the full term.

And even small overpayments can make a big difference. On a 25-year mortgage of £200,000, with an interest rate of 5%, overpaying by just £20 a month could save you £5,700 in interest and clear your debt nine months early, according to Moneycomms.

Overpaying by £50 a month on the same loan would save you £13,400 in interest, and clear the mortgage almost two years early. A £100-a-month overpayment would save £24,530 and clear the debt three years and six months ahead of schedule.

Overpayments don’t have to be on a regular basis. You could pay off a lump sums when you come to the end of your deal, or switch to a new lender, or part-way through if the terms of your loan allow it.

In the above example, a one-off overpayment of £10,000 could save £11,870 in interest and pay off the mortgage one year and two months early.

To make an overpayment, contact your lender. Often it is as simple as making a transfer to the account.

As your overpayments start to make an impact, you will typically be offered the option to reduce either your monthly payments, or the mortgage term. If repayments are comfortable, choose the latter. This means that more of your money goes towards paying off the debt and you’ll clear the balance sooner.

One downside to overpaying is that you can’t easily get the money back if you need it, so ensure you have a savings buffer in case of an emergency; typically three to six months’ of essential outgoings is recommended.

“It’s tempting to try to throw every spare penny at the mortgage, but find a balance between making progress towards being mortgage-free and retaining enough flexibility to deal with life’s unexpected costs,” says David Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C.

Understand the terms of your mortgage: most let you overpay up to 10% of the outstanding balance each year without charges. Hollingworth says: “It’s worth checking as early repayment charges can be substantial, often 3-5% of your overpayment, which can erode, or remove, the benefit of the overpayment.”

If you want to overpay without locking away your money, an offset mortgage can be a good alternative to a standard deal. These let you link a savings account to your mortgage. The savings balance is deducted from the amount you owe, reducing the amount of interest you are charged. For example, on a £200,000 mortgage with a savings balance of £10,000, you would be charged interest on £190,000 of the loan.

The trade-off is that you don’t earn interest on your savings, but they are accessible if you need them; any money withdrawn from the account is simply no longer offset from the mortgage balance. So, in the above example, if you withdrew £2,000 from the savings account, you would then be charged interest on £192,000 of the mortgage loan.

David Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C, says: “An offset can suit those with substantial cash savings or who receive lump sum bonuses. It allows your cash to work harder without limiting your ability to draw on it when required.”…

items.lbText:
Experts say the proposed program prioritizes parents in ‘traditional families’, ignoring the flexibility needed that all families need to support themselves

Erica Hall and her husband knew that raising kids wouldn’t be cheap.

They intentionally had their children five years apart because paying for two in daycare would have been too expensive. When her first child was born, Hall had to self-fund her maternity leave by drawing on savings. And recently, Hall was laid off from her tech job, leaving her at a crossroads.

“Do we move to a lower-cost daycare? What kind of job should I look for? Can I dial back now?” said Hall, who lives in Seattle. And perhaps the most essential of all questions: “Do we need to completely 100% replace my income?”

More American families than ever consist of two working parents: 52% are dual-income households, compared to 31% in 1975, according to the Pew Research Center. Eight out of 10 of these families say the arrangement has been beneficial to their finances.

Despite this shift in family dynamics, the Trump administration has remained focused on an agenda that emphasizes a “traditional” family structure, where one parent stays home to take care of children.

As part of this agenda, the White House is considering a program that would pay parents $9,000 annually to stay at home, using reallocated funds that are now used for federal programs that typically support single mothers and low-income families, according to the New York Times.

The plan was reportedly proffered by JD Vance, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, who has proclaimed himself a defender of “pro-family” policies. The vice-president penned a Wall Street Journal op-ed in 2021 criticizing federal spending on daycare, claiming that “young children from average, healthy homes can be harmed by spending long hours in childcare.”

“It turns out that normal Americans care more about their families than their jobs, and want a family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap daycare so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force,” he wrote on social media at the time.

As vice-president, Vance has continued to angle himself as a defender of families. “To the radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families across our country, we have a simple message for them: stay the hell away from our kids!” Vance said at the Republican’s midterm convention in September.

But experts and parents who spoke to the Guardian said the proposed program for stay-at-home parents prioritizes a single type of family structure and ignores the flexibility that families need to support themselves and their children.

“Families of all compositions need help right now. All families do. We should not pit families against each other,” said Chandra Childers, a senior policy and economic analyst at the Economic Policy Institute.

For Natalia Goodnow of Pittsburgh, being a stay-at-home mother of two was a temporary choice that allowed her family to save on the cost of childcare while she went back to school and pursued a second master’s degree. After she graduated, she was forced to delay her next job search after graduating because the waitlist for her child’s daycare, like many in the country, had grew significantly after the pandemic.

Now, Goodnow is balancing taking care of her children while also building up her own consulting business, which she believes will afford her flexibility to work around her daughter’s schedule. She doesn’t expect she’ll ever stop working in some capacity.

“I’m not built to be just a stay-at-home parent,” she said,

There’s also a risk to relying on one parent’s income. Even though her family is able to live “somewhat stable” on just her husband’s income, Goodnow said she’s worried that his career as a physician, combined with the responsibility to support the whole family himself, will lead to burnout.

“I have to have a second income stream created to give him flexibility to scale down, because it’s just not sustainable,” she said, pointing out that the proposed $9,000 wouldn’t be enough to match what she would make if she worked.

Jillian Whitlow, a mom of three who is pregnant with her fourth child, wishes at times that she could stay at home to take care of her children, but after launching a successful marketing business, her husband left his job as a mechanic to take care of their kids.

The choice stemmed from practicality. The cost of daycare for her children was greater than their monthly mortgage payment.

Though Whitlow’s family, who live in Texas, is in a better financial place than they’ve ever been, they still feel the pain of rising costs and are still paying off student debt and loans on their mobile home. Still, Whitlow sees the White House’s proposal as an unnecessary interference in personal family decisions.

“I would love it if there was a lot less government in all of our lives,” she said, “I would love it if each individual family had more freedom to make the decisions that they want to make about the best way to raise their families.”

“It should be up to me and my family to make that decision, and not the government pushing me to stay at home,” Goodnow said.

Childcare costs can pose a major financial burden on families. Forty per cent of households, including those that have one parent who works less than full-time, spend an outsized percentage of their income on childcare, according to a recent report from the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality.

The White House’s plan, by reallocating federal funds from the Department of Health and Human Services that have typically gone to low-income, single-parent families, could actually making childcare even more expensive or less available, Childers said.

“The minute you start draining resources that go into funding this childcare pool, then rates have to rise on other families, some of whom may already be stretching to make it as it is,” she said.…

items.lbText:
A temporary injunction in the coastline battle for beaches to be publicly accessible, not sealed off for private developments, is just a step in fighting what islanders call a tourism model that disadvantages Jamaicans

W hen the Australian human rights lawyer Eva Buzo emerged from the sea on to the shores of One Man Beach in Montego Bay on Sunday after her gruelling, nearly 11-hour-long swim, the thunderous pulse of welcome drums was drowned out by the chants of “free beach” from jubilant supporters.

Here in Jamaica’s tourism capital, against a backdrop of jagged mountains and sunset-tinted clouds, Buzo – a celebrated marathon swimmer – said she was pleased to help support the important work of the Jamaica Beach Birthright Environmental Movement (Jabbem) and others fighting for free public access to Jamaica’s beaches.

“People’s rights are more important these days than ever, and people keep on trying to encroach on our fundamental freedoms,” she said, calling the privatisation of beaches a colonial legacy. But for Jabbem, her swim was not the most significant milestone this month in its fight for public access.

That came earlier in October, when Jabbem celebrated a rare victory in one of several court cases to end the 1956 Beach Control Act that had given the state ownership of the island’s foreshore and seabed. The act has allowed successive administrations to restrict access to beaches and sell off coastlines to wealthy luxury hoteliers.

In October, however, the court issued an injunction preventing the government from continuing to restrict access to Little Dunn’s River in St Ann while the case continues.

“This victory means a lot for the Jamaican people. It means that our case is strong,” said Dr Devon Taylor, an immunologist with a PhD in biochemistry, who founded Jabbem in 2020.

Wilbourn Carr, 73, who is involved in another fight for beach access in Portland parish, in Jamaica, said the temporary injunction offered hope for other cases.

“The matter of beach access is right across Jamaica. And we just had some success at Little Dunn’s River with that injunction. It gives us hope. Because the fact is that one judge now believes that Jamaicans should have access ,” he said.

The Jamaican government has said it will appeal. In an interview, the environment minister, Matthew Samuda, said there was no basis for protest. He said the government was safeguarding critical tourism investment and protecting communities from crime, while improving beach access through updated legislation requiring future developments to create access points and investment in community leisure spaces.

In the case of Little Dunn’s River, Samuda said access had been restricted after a murder.

“Because of the cultural sensitivity and the love that certain residents of St Ann and those who travel far and wide to come to the facility have for the space, the government intervened and said it would put up appropriate security structures and would facilitate free access to this area on a weekend basis, Friday, Saturday and Sunday,” he said, describing this as “structured management” that also provided benefits such as lifeguards.

Describing tourism as the “largest foreign exchange earner” and the main source of income for nearly 200,000 Jamaicans, Samuda accused activists of portraying the industry as “the enemy”.

He said: “176,000 people aren’t protesting anything to do with beach access, but 176,000 people are feeding their families because of our tourism product … Let’s not put their needs and their concerns on one side.”

Taylor, however, rejected crime prevention as justification for beach closures, pointing out that “the Beach Control Act of 1956 predates the level of crime seen in Jamaica and was never a tool to control crime”. He referred to the Little Dunn’s River restrictions as an illegal “collective punishment of the Jamaican people” that had nothing to do with solving an alleged murder.

“So you could close it until forever, until you solve this murder, which you have not solved,” he said. “You present no evidence that this place was still under threat … So we refute Little Dunn’s River was closed to solve some murder or to stop more from happening, because four years later you only allow the people to use it on Saturdays and Sundays. We deserve leisure seven days a week.”

Paul Roberts, a British architect living in Jamaica and Jabbem’s St Ann community coordinator, argued that the government is creating a false impression that Jamaicans cannot be trusted.

“It’s a load of rubbish,” he said. “I’ve been coming here for 15 years now and I’ve never had any trouble. I’ve never been robbed, I’ve never been mugged and I’ve never faced any issues.”

Campaigners did not oppose hotels, Taylor said, but rather a “plantation tourism” model that disadvantaged Jamaicans.

“Cheap labour of the Jamaican people, degradation of the environment, exclusion of the Jamaican people from the foreshore, plantation tourism, untenable working conditions. Lock us out using colonial-era law. The industry is guilty of that,” he said.

“We the people do not want to be treated as second-class citizens in our country … we want fairness, equality and equity.”

Buzo described access to shared public spaces as a human rights issue, pointing to countries such as Australia, where she is from, and Barbados in the Caribbean that maintain public beach access alongside thriving tourism industries.

“There’s no reason why hotels can’t have beachfront properties that then front on to a public beach. It’s just this kind of exclusivity and segregation that small amounts of people think they need,” she said.

Samuda argued Jamaica was different because, although the country had “conquered our crime monster”, it had “spent 30 years being in the top three most murderous countries on the planet”.…

The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history

Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the Tesla Diner in Los Angeles , Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.

Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.

Musk’s spending is a staggering example of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO’s political influence, as he seeks to help Donald Trump’s administration retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, though current polls predict Democrats achieving a majority. The contributions are at a scale that is difficult to fathom and dwarf efforts from big name megadonors like George Soros or Michael Bloomberg, setting a new precedent for how the rich and powerful attempt to shape politics.

Only last year, Musk claimed he would step away from making large scale political donations after putting nearly $300m towards Trump’s 2024 presidential election campaign. FEC data since then shows he has not only leaned back into financing campaigns, but that his spending has dramatically ramped up as election day approaches, increasing by about $200m in the final two months of campaigning.

Musk’s money has primarily flowed into several Republican-aligned Super Pacs , with his largest contribution of $216m going into his own America Pac. The Pac has targeted 43 House and Senate races across the US, blanketting voters with television commercials, digital ads, text messages and mailers.

America Pac made 839 independent expenditures in House races and 623 in Senate races in 17 states across the country . The spending varies greatly depending on the state, however, with campaigns in battlegrounds such as Michigan and Arizona receiving more of the Pac’s support.

Musk’s Pac has spent the most in his home state of Texas, where a closely fought Senate contest between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton has turned into the most expensive race of the midterms. America Pac has overall poured more than $33m into efforts to elect Paxton, while Musk also made a $168m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund which supports the Paxton campaign.

A large portion of America Pac’s output focuses on attack ads against Democratic candidates such as Talarico, often accusing them of being radical socialists or targeting them over supporting transgender rights. The Pac has spent $28m on anti-Talarico content, including between $300,000 and 350,000 in October on a single Google ad targeting the Texas Senate candidate.

“James Talarico supports parents being charged with child abuse if they do not support transitioning their children,” stated the ad, which was shown more than 10m times over an eight day period.

Musk has also reposted America Pac’s content to his more than 200m followers on X, the social media platform he owns. One of Musk’s posts in October amplified an America Pac attack ad and claimed: “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”

The nearly $446m that Musk has donated this election cycle far exceeds his contributions in the 2024 presidential race, when the tech mogul also held rallies and appeared on stage next to Trump during the campaign. While Musk has been a less visible presence in the midterms, potentially reflecting the US public’s dislike of him , behind the scenes he has greatly upped his financial support for Republicans.

Musk’s spending far outpaces all other donors in the elections, including fellow tech and finance moguls like Marc Andreessen, who also started his own Super Pac. Musk has put more money into this election cycle than what every top Silicon Valley donor, including himself, spent on the 2024 presidential election combined.

The stakes of the midterm elections are potentially high for Musk, who has closely aligned himself with the Trump administration and benefited from its lax policies toward regulating tech and artificial intelligence. SpaceX has also intertwined itself into the government more extensively, landing lucrative contracts this year for Trump’s missile defense program and the use of Musk’s Grok AI chatbot in the Pentagon.

Despite the immense and unprecedented scale of Musk’s political spending, his contributions this election are still only a tiny fraction of the centibillionaire’s overall assets.

Police scheme in City of London offers errant cyclists a choice – watch a roadside safety video or pay a £50 penalty

W hen Aman cycled through a red light in the City of London this week, he was surprised when the police pulled him over. He was positively shocked when, instead of giving him a fine, officers took him into a gazebo to watch a bike safety film.

Aman was one of 30 cyclists caught in the first 20 minutes that morning, as part of a new scheme by City of London police to dissuade cyclists from running red lights.

Many concerned pedestrians have celebrated the time-out zone and, perhaps more surprisingly, cyclists have too.

The new pop-up scheme, called “stop, look, listen, change”, gives offending riders the chance to view an educational film about the dangers of red light jumping. Those caught by police who do not want to pay a £50 fine are taken to a “sin bin” by the roadside, where they watch testimonies from visually impaired road users.

“It is about taking that time away,” said Rob McTaggart, media and engagement manager at City of London police. “Time they didn’t stay waiting for the light is now the time they’re having to spend watching the video. It’s a bit of instant justice in that regard.”

As cyclists continued to be corralled into the time-out zone, McTaggart said the police team had noticed no difference between the numbers of red light runners on hired e-bikes versus those on regular bicycles.

When the sin bin was first launched two weeks ago, roughly 70 people were brought in within90 minutes, McTaggart said. None of the halted riders opted to take the fine.

Watching the safety film, McTaggart said, was useful for spreading road education.

“Right now you can jump on a bike without any training whatsoever,” he said. “It’s about that understanding that just because you can go, it doesn’t mean you should go. We’re not going to enforce our way out of it.”

Sgt Stuart Ford, who helped create the scheme, said it was inspired by the Exchanging Places initiative , where cyclists are brought into large goods vehicles to understand risks like blind spots and difficulties in manoeuvring.

Ford said he was sympathetic to cyclists – “You can quote me: I like bikes” – but added that police “get more complaints than anything else in the city around cyclists jumping lights and their behaviour”. He added: “I’m afraid to say it but a lot of the time, the cyclist is the protagonist here.”

Ford collaborated with the National Federation of the Blind UK (NFBUK) to understand how vulnerable road users are affected by riders skipping lights or riding on the pavement.

Hyacinth Malcolm, who is fully blind, said: “I’m just lost for words as to why they [cyclists] are behaving the way they’re behaving.”

Malcolm said she had to rethink before going out for a daily coffee because of the risk of cyclists colliding with her.

Sarah Leadbetter, a disability activist with visual impairments, also said the footways were not safe for disabled people and that things were getting worse.

She said she relied on a cane, her guide dog and the rotating cone at pedestrian crossings – a small, unassuming plastic or metal cone which is attached to the underside of the push-button unit.

But, she said, she could not be certain of her safety because cyclists “suddenly come through the red light and go straight into you”.

McTaggart said the scheme had sparked discussions across the country and that there was a “huge appetite for what we’re doing here”. In the last week, pedestrians have complained of cyclists riding through the recently pedestrianised Oxford Street.

Sarah Gayton, street access campaign coordinator from NFBUK, commended the new education scheme, but hoped to see the fine increased to £300 and further action taken by the government. “Something has got to give,” she said. “We need designs that work for everybody.”

While some have pitted cyclists and pedestrians against each other, Tom Fyans, CEO of the charity London Cycling Campaign, said he also wanted to see more changes in London’s road designs to better suit all road users.

Standing at the busy junction of Old Street roundabout in the east of the capital, he said: “London isn’t designed for cycling, it’s getting better, but it’s designed for cars. What we need to see is far more cycle-friendly, pedestrian-friendly designs where the car is less important. Then you’ll see a much safer environment for everybody.”

On the new scheme, Fyans said his charity supported the measures over what he believed to be ineffective monetary penalties. He said: “Punishing cyclists with fines and criminal prosecutions, it doesn’t really work. But getting them to think about their impact on other road users – hearts and minds – is much better.”

Fyans said most cyclists do follow the Highway Code, but that a focus on bicycle users was “disproportionate” and a result of the rising number of bike users on London’s roads.

“I think there’s double standards quite often,” he said. “We’re not the biggest danger. It’s cars and speeding and drivers not paying attention that kill people on our roads. That’s the biggest challenge that needs addressing.”

Fyans, who works with Wheels for Wellbeing – a cycling disability group – said he understood the dangers for visually impaired pedestrians and wheelchair users.

But can relations between cyclists and pedestrians be improved? “Let’s address it, but let’s be proportionate about what the real problem is,” he said. “Cyclists are not really the main problem on the road when it comes to danger.”

items.title: Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about it | Carly Dober
items.author: Carly Dober
items.content:
Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom

Ever longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, a new AI personal agent. Unlike traditional chatbots, this little AI tool will be able to fill out forms for you, organise calendars, pay bills and make reservations. Meta describes Muse as a personal agent “built for everyone”. The launch comes at a time when AI agents have been making headlines for hacking into government websites, public agencies and businesses. However, my immediate concern is a little closer to home.

I work as a psychologist, and I’m often talking to clients about lifestyle habits that lead to short-term gain but incur long-term pain. Our brains have a beautiful way of preferring the path of least resistance, of doing what is easiest to preserve our resources. And with the demands of modern life feeling so overwhelming for so many people, the urge to scroll after a long week or defer to a chatbot because you are exhausted is incredibly seducing.

Carly Dober is a psychologist living and working in Melbourne

Jason Hollands, managing director at wealth manager Evelyn Partners, describes the higher rates as a “sting in the tail” for savers.

items.lbText:
John Healey’s budget offered a ‘sting in the tail’ for savers by raising tax rates but there are ways to ease the pain

S avers were both winners and losers in Wednesday’s budget . In his first outing as chancellor, John Healey dropped a plan to cut the cash Isa limit for under-65s but surprised everyone with an extra tax charge on savings and property income. His predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had already announced a plan to increase the income tax rates for savers and landlords that was due to take effect in April 2027. But Healey went further, adding an additional two percentage points to each of the rates.

Jason Hollands, managing director at wealth manager Evelyn Partners, describes the higher rates as a “sting in the tail” for savers.

However, he says: “There are practical steps savers can consider to mitigate this interest tax crunch, although the right approach will depend on their circumstances.”

The levels of tax, which will apply to savers across the UK, will be 24% for basic-rate taxpayers, 44% for higher-rate taxpayers and 49% for those on the additional rate. They come into effect on 6 April.

This means it will get harder to find savings accounts that beat inflation – especially if, as expected, that stays high next year.

Anna Bowes, personal finance expert at advice firm The Private Office, says if inflation hits 3.5%, with the new tax to pay, a saver who pays basic-rate tax will need to earn 4.61% gross interest to retain the value of their money.

A higher-rate payer will need 6.25% gross, and an additional-rate taxpayer will need 6.86%. Currently, she says, these higher two rates “are impossible as far as I am aware” to find on a standard savings account.

There are, however, allowances you can use that will protect some savings, meaning you can beat inflation with a lower-paying account.

Most people can earn a chunk of interest from their savings without facing any tax bill. You don’t have to pay tax on anything earned on money held in cash Isas , and the maximum amount you can put into one in each tax year is going to stay at £20,000.

This was set to be slashed to £12,000 for anyone aged under 65 from April 2027. But Healey has ditched that plan.

Aside from Isas, other things come into play that reduce the tax you pay on savings, or mean you don’t pay any tax at all.

Your tax-free personal allowance covers all of your income, and for the 2026-27 tax year, this is £12,570.

If your personal allowance isn’t fully used up by your wages, pension or other income, HM Revenue and Customs will apply it to your savings interest.

And there are two more savings allowances that people can benefit from.

There’s the personal savings allowance (PSA), which means basic-rate taxpayers can receive £1,000 of interest each financial year without paying any tax, and higher-rate taxpayers can receive up to £500. Additional-rate taxpayers don’t get any PSA.

Until a few years ago, you would usually have needed to have a huge amount saved before exceeding the £500 or £1,000 threshold, but with accounts currently paying 5%-plus, it is much easier to get caught out.

There’s also the “starting rate for savings,” which some people on a low income can get on top of the PSA, where you can earn up to £5,000 of interest without paying tax on it. To benefit, the rest of your income (for example, wages or pension) has to be less than £17,570 a year.

The Isa allowance governs how much you put in each year while the PSA is based on how much you get back.

How quickly you use up the PSA depends on your tax position. A basic-rate taxpayer who puts £20,000 cash into a non-Isa savings account paying 5% interest will earn annual interest of exactly £1,000 – so will use up their entire PSA. If they found a higher paying account, they would face 24% tax on all the interest over £1,000, so they’d hand over 24p of every £1.

For a higher-rate taxpayer it would only take £10,000 in the same account to wipe out their £500 PSA. They would pay a rate of 44% on everything they earned over £500 – 44p in the £1.

When it comes to Isas you can put in up to £20,000 every tax year, as long as you are over 18. Once money is in a cash Isa it is protected from tax forever, so over time you can build up a huge amount of savings that don’t attract tax, as long as you don’t withdraw them.

You do not have to leave it with the same provider. You can move around to get better rates – subject to individual account rules – so it is wise to make the most of this shelter.

If you have a substantial savings nest egg you might want to review where they are held. Experts always recommend that you have emergency funds that are easy to access, so do not let a small tax bill deter you from doing that.

But Hollands says it is worth checking that you are not holding too much in savings. “Holding more cash than you need for several years can mean missing out on the potential for longer-term investment growth,” he says.

Look at your family situation. Hollands says couples who are married, or in a civil partnership, should look at their savings and allowances together.

If you have both used your Isa and personal savings allowances, but one partner pays tax at a lower rate, he says transferring cash to them could reduce an overall family tax bill.

“But this needs to be a genuine transfer: the money becomes theirs, legally and in practice, and they must be free to decide what to do with it, so trust is key,” he says.

If you’re saving for a child’s future, consider putting it in their name instead of holding it yourself. Pay into their child trust fund, or junior Isa if they already have one, or set up a junior Isa. You can pay up to £9,000 a year into a junior Isa, and all the returns are tax-free.…

Sellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fall

Eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price, according to research by Coutts, which provides private banking services to wealthy clients.

Property prices in “prime central London”, which covers the city’s most expensive postcodes, have dropped 5% in the third quarter of 2026, as the slowdown in the UK’s property market hits its wealthiest residents.

It means some affluent people are facing hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of pounds in losses to the value of their homes, with properties selling at an average 10% discount to their asking price, Coutts found.

Prices in the highest end of London’s property market are now 14% below their peak in 2014, having been hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs. Buying and selling agents in the capital have also reported a slowdown in interest from foreign-born buyers after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.

Exclusive areas such as Knightsbridge and Belgravia, and South Kensington have been hit the hardest, Coutts said, with prices 30.8% and 26.9% below their peaks respectively.

Alex Webster, head of lending at the bank, said buyers and sellers at the top end of the market were taking a more cautious approach, even before the chancellor, John Healey’s, first budget this week.

Sellers will now be watching to see if the budget “encourages some of that delayed activity to return”, she said. “But financing conditions and the wider economic environment will continue to influence the market.”

There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.

While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week its monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.

In the meantime, sellers in prime central London are increasingly shying away, Coutts found, with new listings down 14% compared with the previous quarter and available stock down by 6% year-on-year.

Transactions were 9.1% lower in the third quarter of this year, it said, with the biggest slowdown in the £2m-£5m band, where transactions were down 22.3%.

However, separate research from the estate agent Savills found that buyers at the very top end of the market are driving activity, with 26 transactions above £10m in the third quarter of this year, taking the total to 127 over the past year. Together, these sales were worth £2.88bn, it found.

items.lbText:
The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia

The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.

The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia .

The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 with an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.

For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.

It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.

The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.

At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.

On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.

“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”

The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.

“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”

Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.

One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube , including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.

“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.

Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.

The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.

“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.

Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.…

items.title: Soaring cost of Halloween treats spooks shoppers
items.content: <article>The price of candy, especially chocolate, is up, and Halloween bargain hunters are searching for deals and ways to cut costs. </article>
items.lbText:
Halloween shoppers in the US seeking sweet relief this spooky season have instead been shocked by the high price of seasonal treats, as cost of living pressures continue to bite.

Demetrio Beltres, a 33-year-old financial adviser searching for Halloween bargains for trick or treaters said he was spending more than his usual $15 (£11) to $20 this year because prices were much higher.

"I'm trying to spend at least $20 to $30 just to make sure that I get the kids something," he said, while browsing the rows of colour options at a Target in Manhattan.

A lot of people are finding they are in the same boat as Demetrio this year.

Stephen Zagor, adjunct associate professor at Columbia Business School, said people have only so much to spend, and when everyday essentials are costing more, people may feel less inclined to make this the most extravagant Halloween.

"I think the holiday's gotten scary, more from an economic [perspective], than it might be for scaring people at the door," he said.

Analysis from left-leaning non-profit Groundwork Collaborative and the Century Foundation found the cost of popular Halloween chocolates and confectionery was 15.3% higher this year than in 2025.

Separate research from personal finance firm Finance Buzz found prices for Halloween treats have soared by 71% over the past five years - a much bigger increase than the general pace of price rises over the same period.

The price of confectionery generally has been pushed up thanks to higher cocoa prices.

The cost of a tonne of cocoa skyrocketed to a high of more than $10,700 in January 2025, according to figures from the International Monetary Fund via the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis, as climate change contributed to severe weather which affected supplies.

"The cocoa that is now being consumed was bought when the prices were high," said Zagor, who specialises in food businesses.

Cost of living pressures have also increased, with inflation running at 3.7%, and fuel prices remain high. Diesel, at $6.32 a gallon, is only 20 cents below the record reached in September.

People shopping for Halloween treats in New York were noticing the price pressures.

"Everything is expensive, so it does not surprise me that Halloween candy is expensive too," said Mallory, who declined to give her last name.

The combined cost of living pressures have affected how much people are buying in the run up to the holiday, according to consumer and market research company Nielsen IQ. It found Halloween treat sales were down 11.7% by the middle of September, and by the middle of October sales were down 6.7%.

Chris Costagli, NielsenIQ's vice-president of US food thought leadership, said shoppers appeared more willing to spend as Halloween neared, but remained cautious.

"Sales have improved considerably from where we started in September, with smaller packs gaining ground while larger sizes continue to struggle," he said.

"This feels like a consumer who still wants the occasion, but is paying much closer attention to what goes into the basket."

Zagor, who is a fan of Halloween as well as traditional Halloween treats, said cutting back on costs, could present a good opportunity to offer trick or treaters a different kind of experience when they come to your door.

"It could be how you present the candy when kids come to your house as much as the one piece of candy that you're going to give," he said.

Options could include using a spooky fake skeleton hand to share out treats, rather than letting children reach into a bowl, or dressing up to meet trick or treaters.

Zagor said making your own treats is another option, inviting people over to make them together.

"You could certainly do something slightly magical, slightly interesting," he suggested.

"The trick literally could be as important as the treat."

items.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
items.content: <article>The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.</article>
items.lbText:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.

The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.

Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.

The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.

While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.

The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.

Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".

It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."

Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".

Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.

In a later update, the firm set it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.

The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.

Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.

Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.

The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.

A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.

The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.

But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.

Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.

Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".

Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.

In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.

In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.

Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.

North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.

North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.

It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

items.title: Suspicious bets returning £149,000 for predicting Ballon d’Or under investigation
items.author: Ed Aarons and Romain Molina
items.content:
• Bets predicted exact top-five men’s finishing order

A series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order of this year’s Ballon d’Or and generated almost $200,000 (£149,000) in winnings is being investigated by the event’s organisers, France Football, who have also contacted the police.

It has been alleged that 12 Polymarket accounts – an American cryptocurrency-based prediction market – placed the bets, with more than $264,000 wagered on the outcome before Monday’s ceremony. Their extraordinary accuracy has raised serious questions about a potential leak of confidential results before football’s most prestigious individual award. Harry Kane was crowned the winner at the ceremony at the London Palladium, finishing ahead of Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Lionel Messi. Remarkably, this was the exact order predicted by the group of accounts identified in French media outlet Upside’s investigation.
